Obesity increases the likelihood of an individual suffering from depressive symptoms due to worsened body image and social isolation. This may lead to further health concerns, such as suicide.

PVD is characterised by worsened blood flow to the limbs of an individual caused by the build-up of plaque in an unhealthy diet. a) patients with asthma benefit greatly from participating in both low-impact aerobic training and strength/resistance training. It is also important to note that asthmatics should always have a ventilator available. Ventolin helps to open up the airways of the individual which are normally quite constricted allowing for more air to get through and access all parts of the body, especially the working muscles during exercise. Participating in aerobic exercises 2-3 times a week can also help improve the airways of the individual by getting the muscles of the diaphragm and lungs working more often. Strength training is a good way to keep physically active without putting too much strain on the lungs as slow and controlled breathing can typically be maintained during the movements. It is important to avoid activities that will cause dyspnea as this can result in severe asthma, possibly leading to an asthma attack

b) specific respiratory muscle training helps to strengthen the muscles of the lungs and airways. Not only does it strengthen them but it also increases their size. The bigger the alveoli and bronchioles are, the bigger the surface area is which significantly increases the amount of air that can be diffused into and out of the lungs therefore increasing the amount of oxygen that gets sent around the body. This can not only improve asthma and exercise-induced asthma, it can also improve respiratory conditions such as cystic fibrosis as it helps to increase the dilation of the airways.¬†

a) obesity is the condition diagnosed by individual's BMI being greater than 35 and their waist circumference being greater than 80cm for females and 84cm for males. These measurements indicate the amount of visceral fat on an individual. Obese individuals will have a high level of visceral fat. This condition is an important risk factor for many chronic health conditions. The higher the level of obesity is, the more at risk the individual is indicating why it is such an important health concern and is typically one of the first that specialists and doctors will address. By lowering an individual's weight, the risks of developing these diseases also decreases.

b) some of the co-morbidities of obesity are type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease and hypertension. Individuals who are obese have a significantly higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes as the bodys ability to regulate glucose and produce insulin is impacted. The body becomes insulin resistant and so the glucose in the body can't break down, leading to high blood glucose levels as well as the risk of hyperglycaemia. This can be very dangerous and can lead to permanent health conditions and death. Obesity can also impact the ability of the heart to work. the more visceral fat on the body, the harder the heart has to work to pump blood around the body, putting more strain on the heart which can lead to many other cardiovascular diseases such as myocardial infarction and heart failure. Individual's with obesity typically have more plaque build up in their arteries which can also put strain on the heart as it has to work harder to pump enough blood as there is less room for the blood to move through the arteries. This can lead to atherosclerosis which increases the risk of hypertension and coronary heart disease. These conditions can further impact the individual's health and wellbeing, limiting their ability to perform activities of daily living and lowering their quality of life.¬†

c) increasing the accessibility and resources for exercise such as gyms and parks will more than likely increase the likelihood of individual's seeking out more physical activity. By providing more social settings such as run clubs and groups people may find it easier to put themselves out there and work to improve their functional capacity and participate in more physical activity. They could also implement more healthy eating habits by providing easier ways to access healthy foods and make them cheaper as one main factor that plays into unhealthy eating habits is the inability to afford health foods as well as be able to cook at home and provide better meals for themselves. Alongside this, providing a few free/cheap or easily accessible cooking classes or healthy ready made meals can help people participate in healthier eating habits, improving their diet and lowering the risk of developing obesity and also losing weight for those who already are obese.¬†

A) Asthma is typically induced by the increase in respiratory demand, especially in a cooler and dryer environment. This then leads to constriction of the airways and change in osmolarity of the lining of the respiratory pathway, creating more mucus and further constricting the airway.

Increasing overall cardiovascular health also leads to strengthening the respiratory system, overall decreasing the load on the respiratory system in higher intensities of exercise. Cardiovascular fitness exercises such as running and biking are beneficial to asthmatic individuals however, swimming is considered to be the most beneficial due to the high humidity of the air.

Similarly, is good for asthmatic individuals to avoid exercise at cooler and dryer environments such as, early in the morning, during winter, at high altitudes. Lower altitudes and overall higher humidity in the air helps to prevent the onset of asthmatic symptoms.

Inhalors such as ventolin make breathing easier by expanding the passage for air to pass through in and out of the lungs, preventing wheezing, coughing and other asthma symptoms as air is able to more easily enter the lungs without airway constriction or obstruction. Breathing whilst contracting the core is also an exercise to assist the treatment of respiratory conditions as individuals practice breathing in and out while focusing on engaging the abdominal muscles and contracting the diaphragm. This mimicks the breathing technique used during physical exertion, thus helping asthmatic individuals with breathing control when engaging in physical activity.

column48: Adherence to exercise relies on an individual's free willingness to complete exercise programs and their contributions to its success.¬† The 5 main contributors to adherence include physical, psychological, environmental, social and behavioural tendencies. Physical tendencies are underpinned by an individual's ability to complete exercise that is prescribed to them, therefore if intensity or difficulty is too high, the person will not have the physicality necessary for the completion of exercise and will not adhere to the program. Psychological adherence refers to an individuals fear level associated with exercise, which may be due to a past negative experience that resulted in a symptomatic episode or a devasting health event. This will significantly impact an individual's willingness to conform to prescribed exercise, therefore consideration of fears and worries should be taken. Environmental concerns include the physical place where exercise is being done, such as in a gym or on a field, and emotions associated with these places. If an event occurred in a environment that was adverse to an individual's health they may have fears that will impact their adherence to an exercise program, therefore it is essential to consult the patient. Additionally, social factors affect adherence as people have preferences and are more likely to adhere to a program if they are completing it with a friend and use it as a source of social gain rather than solely focusing on the fact that they are exercising. Consideration of the sociable nature of a patient is necessary and group or individual sessions can be prescribed to improve adherence. Finally, behavioural tendencies have a huge impact on adherence as habits will impact an individual's willingness to complete exercise. Habit history will be a major prescriptive variable and habit formation should be an essential consideration to improving a patient's adherence to an exercise program.

a) Strategies to manage asthma includes relieving measures, preventative measures as well as appropriate exercise.¬†

Preventative measures of asthma is to suppress inflammation of the airways and use inhaled or oral corticosteroids, which provide an increased exercise tolerance and capacity when used with long-term bronchodilators. Relieving measures of asthma in the form of medication include bronchodilators which are Ventolin inhalers, which help increase ventilatory capacity and allow for airflow to pass more freely through the airways. Another relieving medication for those with asthma is B2-Adrenoreceptors which ultimately relax the smooth muscle in the airway, further allowing for an increased exercise capacity and an enhanced flow of oxygen through the airways. Airway hydrators are also a great medication as they prevent the dehydration of airways, further enhancing airflow. It is critical that we prescribe exercise that will not trigger the inflammation of the airways nor dehydrate the airways. Exercise such as swimming is highly recommended as it is a humid environment which will not dehydrate the airways. Exercise prescription for asthma includes low-intensity activities such as swimming or walking, performed in humid environments where the air is warm. Avoid exercising in cold, dry climates as this will trigger bronchoconstriction and asthma symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, airflow limitations and shortness of breath. Prescribing Cardiorespiratory exercise 2-3 times a week, with moderate intensities, doing swimming is ideal.¬†

¬†

b) Respiratory muscle training is a technique aimed to increase the function of the inspiratory and expiratory muscles, further increasing the force developed when we inhale and exhale. This training involved an individual breathing against resistance. This training has direct effects of increasing aerobic power of the diaphragm and other respiratory muscles. This training can be useful for obstructive pulmonary diseases such as emphysema, chronic bronchitis, COPD and asthma, as well as restrictive pulmonary diseases such as cystic fibrosis. This training has benefits such as increased oxygen availability, improved cardiac carbon dioxide removal (such as improved lactate removal), improved submaximal responses, larger ability to complete activities of daily living, improved cognitive function, increased quality of life, reductions in symptoms like shortness of breath and tightness in the chest.

a) Obesity is a metabolic disease that is the most common and preventable disease and is where an individual is in a chronic positive energy balance. Obesity is such a health concern as since 1995 the rates of obesity are increasing. Obesity is also concerning as 66% of adults are obese and 26% of children are obese, which are alarming and increasing values. It is also such a concern as it is the most preventable disease through appropriate behavioural, lifestyle, education and exercise interventions.

¬†

B) Co-morbidities of obesity are diabetes (specifically Type 2), hypertension, myocardial infarction and Valvular Disease.¬†

Firstly, Type 2 diabetes relates to obesity as a co-morbidity as an obese individual consumes a diet high in sugar, saturated fat and sodium, which are foods that contribute to an increase in blood glucose. Furthermore, an obese individual will have large and continual increases in blood glucose and high amounts of glucose entering the blood at all times. Furthermore, the beta cells in the pancreas are working hard to produce enough insulin to compensate for the large amounts of glucose in the blood. However, the overproduction of insulin causes the beta cells to become worn out and insufficient insulin is produced, resulting in Type 2 Diabetes. The potential health consequences of Type 2 diabetes leads to poor insulin sensitivity, premature death, increased HR and BP, low exercise capacity, dyslipidaemia, sleep apnoea, cancer.

Hypertension is also a co-morbidity of obesity, as an individual who is obese has higher cholesterol from the consumption of foods high in saturated fat. This saturated fat builds up as plaque on the walls of the arteries, resulting in atherosclerosis, further restricting and limiting blood flow to the brain, heart and skeletal muscles. This restriction in blood flow results in a reduced vascular compliance, further leading to high blood pressure, known as hypertension. Health consequences include increased HR, low insulin sensitivity, severe dyspnoea.

Myocardial Infarction is related to obesity as again, the foods an obese individual consumes are high in saturated fat and LDL cholesterol, further causing stenosis of the blood vessels to occur, which results in the necrosis of cardiomyocytes from a sustained or sudden lack of blood supply. This ischemia results in a heart attack. Health consequences include chest pain, abornormal ECG readings (new pathological Q wave)

Valvular disease is also related to obesity as the valves of the heart are unable to open or close properly and this could be a result of stenosis or occulsion which is the narrowing of blood vessels from thick or stiff valves. These thick valves come from the plaque build up in the valves that are a result of a diet high in saturated fat and a lack of physical activity, which is common in obese individuals. Common health consequences are ventricular overload, ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure.

C) Health interventions can be walking groups where people come together to walk, this further reduces BMI and helps with weight loss. Behavioural interventions surrounding education sessions on how to manage weight through exercise and diet is also beneficial in reducing obesity.

b) Four co-morbidities associated with obesity are hypertension, high cholesterol, peripheral artery disease and coronary heart disease. All of these co-morbidities are associated with the increasing presence of atherosclerosis, which is the buildup of fatty plaque within the blood's channels. Hypertension comes from an increase in sedentary behaviour and the regular choice of high LDL-C foods (fatty and high carbohydrate foods, often fried). This is associated with patients who are obese. High cholesterol also comes from the increased occurrence of poor diet choices and low or no purposeful physical activity. Coronary heart disease, which occurs from stenosis or rupture of an occlusion within the arteries of the heart, is a result of severe atherosclerosis which often occurs for patients who are obese. Peripheral artery disease can cause pain in the lower extremities/limbs of patients who have it. This can encourage sedentary behaviour due to the pain increase. This sometimes can either contribute to obesity originating (within a patient) or be an associated factor with existing obesity (within a patient).

a) Given that asthma is a reversible condition, medications such as Ventilin inhalors cause bronchodilation in the airways. This results in the opening of the airways, allowing more oxygen to travel through to the lungs, enhancing their quality of life (QOL). Exercise can be an effective tool to manage and improve asthma, as it is a natural bronchodilator. However, precaution must be made when prescribing and delivering exercise for asthmatics, as medications such as inhalers must be on the patient at all times during exercise. If airway obstruction symptoms are present, such as shortness of breath or weezing, exercise must temporarily be halted and medication must be administered. If symptoms do not reverse and improve, exercise must be terminated. Some other considerations for exercising with asthmatic is avoiding conditions that promote flare ups, such as cool, dry weather, as well as exercising outdoors in the winter. To counter this, swimming is an excellent mode of exercise for asthmatics due to the high humidity and hydration of airways, as well as incoproating modifications such as warming up with a scarf around the mouth and nose may further hydrate the airways.¬†

B) Respiratory muscle training (RMT) involves the training of respiratory muscles such as the diaphragm to expand and relax more efficiently, leading to greater inhalation and exhalation. With conditions such as asthma and COPD, this is especially important due to the obstructed airways, particularly during exhalation. Thus, exercising to train these muscles, such as relatively high intensity aerobic exercise like walking, running or swimming, decreases the inflammation of airways, as well as strengthens the smooth muscles of these structures. With stronger respiratory muscles, this improves the overall airlfow and exhalation, reducing asthma symptoms.

a) Obesity is the metabolic inflammation of the body, leading to excessive adipose tissue around the body. This inflammation of the body places extensive stress on central and peripheral structures, such as increasing myocardial oxygen demand, reducing lung compliance, promoting atherogenesis, increasing total peripheral resistance, as well as peripheral complications such as excessive joint/bone loading.

b) Obesity is typically not a disease on its own, with obese individuals often presenting with hypertension, coronary artery disease, high levels of visceral fat and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM). Hypertension is the elevated blood pressure at rest, typically involving an increased in total peripheral resistance (TPR). TPR is typically elevated due to atherosclerosis, involving narrowed or blocked arteries, leading to endothelial dysfunction, ultimately causing increased myocardial demand to pump blood around the body, causing a rise in blood pressure. Secondly, coronary artery disease (CAD) is the atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries, which pump blood away from the heart with blood. When these arteries become blocked due to the plaque, occlusions or ruptures can occur, leading to myocardial infarctions or tissue necrosis. Additionally, visceral adipose tissue (VAT) refers to the fat lining the internal organs. This can significantly raise inflammation in the body, as well as increasing LDL-C, causing significant health risks and leading to diseases such as MI or strokes. Lastly, T2DM is the resistance to insulin, whereby the GLUT4 transporters have impaired sensitivity, causing the inability to oxidise and use glucose effectively, or for storage of energy. This insulin resistance can cause significant health complications, such as hyperglycaemia which poses significant risk of cardiovascular disease.

An example of reliever medication includes, ventolin which acts as a bronchodilator, which relaxes smooth muscles, helping expand airways to relieve airway obstruction. For example, it is advisable to avoid dry and cold climates as these can provoke asthma and where possible also avoid pollutants such as smoke. a) Obesity is a metabolic disease where the processing, absorption and distribtution of macronutrients and micronutrients has been impaired due to chronic positive energy balance. Obesity can also be influenced by other factors such as genetic history or enviornmental factors, but a large percentage of diagnosed individuals is a result of consuming more energy than what is expended. Obesity is an important health concern as it is a massive risk factor for other conditions and diseases such as hypertension and cardiovascular disease. As obesity is largely preventable it is important to act early, to prevent the onset of such comorbidities.

b) One co-morbidity of obesity is hypertension or high blood pressure. Many individuals with obesity consume large amounts of cholesterol and saturated fat. This results in the production of poor lipid profiles, and induces astheroclerosis which leads to the development of high blood pressure. Similarly, another comorbidity of obesity is type 2 diabetes. Type 2 diabetes is insulin resistant diabetes that is developed overtime, due to pancreatic beta cells working on overload for chronic periods of time. It is common for individuals with obesity to consume high amounts of sugar in their diet, which causes hyperglycaemia, leading to decreased insulin sensitivity, and diabetes.¬†

Two other morbidities include cardiovascular diseases such as coronary heart disease and heart failure. a) Exercise is an effective treatment for asthmatics. It should be the primary intervention for treatment, before medications. This will, in turn, lessen the symptoms of asthma such as chest tightness and shortness of breath, leading to an improvement in overall health and quality of life.

It is related to obesity through the realm of lifestyle - foods that contribute to adipose tissue build up cause atherosclerotic deposits in the arteries. These can cause acute coronary events and places undue stress on the heart.

Another co-morbidity is hypertension (high BP). It is caused also caused by atherosclerotic plaque build up in the arteries. This increases the stress on the heart. It is related to obesity through lifestyle choices - poor diet and sedentary lifestyle.

Another co-morbidity is peripheral vascular disease, caused by atherosclerotic plaque build up in the arteries away from the heart (mainly legs), also causing arterial narrowing. This can cause ischaemia in the muscles of the extremity and place undue stress on the heart, potentially leading to heart failure or myocardial infarction.

Finally, Type II diabetes is a co-morbidity of obesity. It is caused by decreased insulin sensitivity in cells of the pancreas. This leads to high blood glucose levels (hyperglycaemia) and increased urinary glucose levels (glucosuria). It is a co-morbidity due to both being lifestyle diseases - a result of a sedentary lifestyle and/or high-sugar diet.

The management of asthma through exercise aims to improve functional capacity, improve Vo2max, ventilatory load and overall quality of life. An individual with asthma may compete in any form of exercise however must ensure medications such as an inhalor are readily available if possible adverse affects occur. In obstructive conditions such as asthma, cystic fibrosis and COPD, the airways are blocked due to inflammation and mucus, leading to difficulties exhaling air from the lungs. This can lead to a reduced FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio, primarily affecting the amount of air exhaled in the initial parts of expiration. a) Asthma is considered a reversible airway obstruction. It is an obstructive cardiopulmonary conditions which can make breathing difficult. Asthmatics can generally participate in exercise like any healthy individuals, however, there are certain precautions and strategies that are important to ensure QoL.¬†

Asthmatics should avoid exercising in triggering environments, such as cold and pollutant air. So avoiding exercise in the early mornings or outside during the cold winter is beneficial. If exercising in these environments, the individual should wear a scarf or a mask in front of the mouth to humidify the air they breathe in. This is due to the drying mechanics of the airways that often happen during exercise due to mouth breathing. An exercise that can be very good and accessible for asthmatics is swimming, due to the humid air and also the focus on controlled breathing.

There are different medications used to help manage asthma. For instance, fast-acting bronchodilators are used to relax the smooth muscles surrounding the airways to make it easier to breathe. This is a reliever medication and works rapidly to help manage symptoms immediately. It is recommended that asthmatics always have reliever medications accessible during exercise. There are also preventative medications that work by maintaining a bronchodilation over time. These medications do not provide immediate relief, however, they can prevent exacerbations as it helps keep the airways open. They need to be taken on a regular basis to work.

There is an asthmogenic scale that indicates the likelihood of an activity to trigger symptoms. Walking, swimming, and cycling are all low on this scale and therefore recommended aerobic activities. Other activities that are slightly higher on the scale but may also be great for asthmatics is things like kayaking and running.¬†

Overall, people with asthma can train and compete at high levels. As long as there are reliever medications readily available, it should be okay.¬†

a) Obesity is classified using the BMI scale. The calculation is (mass x height) / height^2. If this calculation is > 25 an individual is considered overweight, and when it is > 30 they are classified as obese. However, this calculation does not take body composition into account, and it can therefore be very misleading for populations such as athletes. BMI scales should therefore be used in combination with measurements such as waist circumference, where a measurement of > 90cm for women, and > 94cm for men is considered obese. Obesity is the second leading risk factors for many chronic conditions, and it can lead to several health concerns.

b) Obesity is a risk factor for several different conditions, such as hypertension, coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, and diabetes.¬†

Obesity increases the risk of dislipidemia, which is a poor lipid profile. Obesity is generally the result of a sustained positive energy balance. This can often be induced by poor diet choices, such as fatty and fried foods. These types of food have high LDL (low-density lipoproteins), which is pro-atherogenic. This means that they contribute to the development of atherosclerosis - fatty deposits (plaque) in the intima space of the arteries, causing the arteries to narrow. This narrowing of the arteries increases the total peripheral resistance which will lead to an increased blood pressure. Hypertension is chronic high BP.¬†

Coronary artery disease and peripheral artery disease have similar mechanics. Coronary artery disease is the narrowing of blood vessels leading into the heart whereas peripheral artery disease is the narrowing of blood vessels in the peripherals, mainly the legs. As with hypertension, this comes from the build-up of atherosclerosis in the vessels, causing the arteries to narrow and making it harder to pump blood effectively. For coronary artery disease, the heart doesn't get blood efficiently, and for peripheral artery disease the heart is forced to work harder to pump blood through the narrowed arteries into the peripherals.¬†

Diabetes is poor glycaemic control. Obesity is often linked to the development of type 2 diabetes. This is an impaired ability of the body to clear glucose from the blood

a) When performing a 12 leads ECG, 6 electrodes which are unipolar, are placed along the chest and above the heart. 3 of the body electrodes, the left arm, right arm and left leg are biopolar leads, that read 2 views of the heart. These also create Einthovens ECG triangle, between the left leg, left arm and right arm. The right leg electrode is used as an anchor. As the 3 electrodes from Einthovens triangle have 2 views, they create 6 leads out of 12.¬†

In conclusion, 6 unipolar electrodes, plus 3 biopolar electrodes, create 12 leads in total and therefore reading 12 leads from 10 electrodes placed on the body.

A) Some appropriate strategies to manage the health and quality of life of asthmatics include: performing exercise in warm and humid clients, limiting exposure to pollutants and providing an adequate warm-up. As exposure cold-dry climates are known to cause Exercise induced asthma exercising in warm and humid climates keeps the airways moist and prevents dehydration and subsequent inflammation and restriction of the airways. Similarly, providing an adequate warm-up would be useful to manage the health and quality of life of asthmatics as it would prevent a sudden increase in ventilatory demand of exercise. This would allow asthmatics to effectively train at higher intensities without being as susceptible to an exercise induced asthmatic event associated with sudden changes in ventilatory demand. Additionally, asthmatics should also become familiar with bronchodilator medications such as ventolin. These medications could be taken during exercise or pre-exercise to restrict bronchoconstriction and reduction of airflow which overall would further reduce the ventilatory requirements of tasks of daily living such as walking up stairs.

B) Respiratory muscle training can assist in the treatment of asthma. As asthma is restrictive it prevents full expansion of the lungs, reducing the ability of individuals to intake adequate oxygen for daily tasks. Exercises such as deep breathing and diaphragm exercises could be useful to train the body to effectively expand the thoracic cage, increasing total volume and allowing for increased oxygen intake. Examples of exercises could include breathing with a focus on filling the stomach first and then moving up to the chest. Regarding COPD respiratory muscle training would also be useful to increase the quality of life. Some exercises could include blowing through a tube to push light hollow balls into the air. This would effectively train the costal muscles to contract more forcefully, while this may not restore original function it can maintain the level of respiratory abiltiy they currently have. Similiarly, teaching COPD patients proper coughing technique can help with the removal of sputum which increases airway resistance. Strategies to manage health and quality of life involve exercise, as well as medications which can relieve and prevent asthma attacks.

Exercise is a key strategy, however asthma can also be induced by exercise due to dehydration, hence when exercises it is important that the environment is warm and humid to avoid dehydration of airways. Swimming is a great from of exercise to increase health, and aerobic capacity whilst eliminates being in a dry environment. Swimming also helps an asthmatic individual regulate and control their breathing which is beneficial for respiratory muscle training as well.

a) Asthma is a cardiopulmonary condition characterised by an inflammation of the airways. Various strategies can be implemented to manage health and quality of life. Bronchodilators are a type of medication that can be taken to improve an individual's vasodilation and reduce constriction of the airways. This will improve airflow, allowing an asthmatic to maximise their oxygen intake along with the amount that is able to be absorbed by the bloodstream. As a cardiopulmonary condition, the main aim of these strategies are to improve an individual's functional capacity. In order to do this, aerobic and resistance training can be prescribed. We want to aim for 3-5 aerobic sessions per week, at a moderate intensity, along with 2-3 resistance sessions per week, focusing on low load, yet high repetitions. ¬†3-5 aerobic sessions at a moderate intensity, roughly 40-70% of VO2 max, can be prescribed for an athlete. Whilst many athletes with asthma can progress to performing at a professional level, it is important to be conservative when prescribing exercise initially, especially for unfit individuals. It is also vital that we monitor the athlete's oxygen saturation levels in doing so. For example, we may prescribe the athlete 3 sessions a week, on every second day, encompassing 30 minutes of incline walking at a moderate pace on a treadmill, aiming for approximately 70% of heart rate max. For a 50 year old client, we can calculate heart rate max by subtracting their age from 220, which is 170. 70% of this would be roughly 119 beats per minute. We can increase or decrease this goal based on subjective and objective responses from the client, such as heart rate, VO2 max, blood pressure and rate of perceived exertion.

b) Specific muscle training can assist in the treatment of asthma and other respiratory conditions, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cystic fibrosis. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease manifests in a similar way to asthma, with clients presenting similar symptoms that negatively affect their quality of life. Both are characterised by airway obstructions. It is important to prescribe specific respiratory muscle training for these conditions, to ensure maximum efficiency and benefits for the athlete, whilst ensuring safety and comfort/enjoyment for the athlete. For these conditions, we want to apply muscle training in the form of low load and high repetitions. We are not trying to improve cardiovascular function but rather an individual's functional capacity to absorb as much oxygen as possible, with limited restriction. By implementing high repetitions with low load, we aren't placing immense strain on the cardiopulmonary system, however we are encouraging the body to adapt to the demands of exercise, improving the flow of oxygen around the body, in turn reducing blood pressure.¬†

1) One strategy to improve health and quality of life (QoL) for asthmatics is the use of medication. Long acting bronchodilators may be used at set periods throughout the day as a measure to prevent/reduce asthmatic symptoms, whilst short acting bronchodilators such as Ventolin may be utilised to reduce symptoms during a bout of increased asthmatic symptoms, such as exercise induced asthma (EIA). Inhaled corticosteroids may also be used to reduce inflammation of the airways and inhibit the immune response responsible for excess mucous production in the airways. Exercise, specifically of an aerobic nature, has also been shown to be useful tool to reduce asthmatic symptoms and improve quality of life, such as increasing the workload at which asthmatic symptoms present, therefore allowing ADLs and more exercise to be performed without discomfort. However, a number of key considerations must be noted. Firstly, bronchodilators should always be present in case of a bout of EIA, and exercise should be terminated if symptoms are not relieved via the use of this. The environment must also be considered to reduce the incidence of exercise induced asthma. Cold, dry environments should be avoided, as well as environments with high levels of air pollution and allergens (specific to each individual). Indoor swimming may be utilised to avoid these triggers, due to the warm humid air and indoor environment (less pollutants/allergens). A gradual warm up should also be included, as evidence suggests that this will result in a lower incidence of EAI, compared to beginning at the main session workload/intensity.

b) Specific respiratory muscle training may be useful to increase the strength of the respiratory muscles. This will allow for more forceful inhalation and expiration, which is useful for asthma and other obstructive and restrictive diseases. It will also decrease the relative intensity of breathing for the respiratory muscles and decrease their demand for oxygen. This will allow for oxygen to be supplied to larger working muscles and improve performance of ADLs.

a) Obesity is defined as having a BMI greater than or equal to 30. It is an important health concern as it is a risk factor for many chronic health diseases, such as Cardiovascular disease (CVD), hypertension and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM). Individuals with obesity also have higher rates of all-cause mortality, resulting in a lower life-expectancy compared to a non-obese individual.

b)

1. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus- Individuals with obesity are on average consuming more energy than is required, causing an increase in adipose tissue due to a chronic positive energy balance. When carbohydrate is consumed, insulin must be released by the pancreas to initiate the process of cellular uptake of blood glucose. If the positive energy balance is caused by an overconsumption of carbohydrate, the pancreas must produce large amounts of insulin, which the cells of the body eventually become less sensitive to, causing a decrease in insulin sensitivity. This causes a positive feedback loop, where blood glucose remains high, causing the pancreas to produce more insulin, eventually wearing out the Beta cells and leading to a relative and absolute deficiency of insulin, requiring insulin injections for the affected person to maintain normal blood glucose levels. Some potential health consequences include macrovascular and microvascular disease, diabetic neuropathy and hyper/hypoglycaemic incidents.

2. Coronary Heart Disease- individuals with obesity tend to have poor lipid profiles due to an increased consumption of foods high in saturated fats and refined carbohydrates causing a chronic positive energy balance. Obesity may also cause poor metabolism of fats and carbohydrates, which may also worsen the lipid profile. Low HDL-C and high LDL-C can lead to growing atherosclerotic deposits in the intimal layer of the coronary artery. This may lead to an occlusion of one or more of the coronary arteries, resulting in ischemia and potential infarction of myocardial tissue.

3. Hypertension- ¬†individuals with obesity tend to have poor lipid profiles due to an increased consumption of foods high in saturated fats and refined carbohydrates causing a chronic positive energy balance. Obesity may also cause poor metabolism of fats and carbohydrates, which may also worsen the lipid profile. Low levels of HDL-C and high levels of LDL-C may lead to atherosclerotic deposits in the intimal wall of arteries throughout the body. This may lead to a stenosis of one or more arteries, causing increased total peripheral resistance and therefore increasing blood pressure.

4. Peripheral artery disease- Individuals with obesity may have poor lipid profiles due to the reasons stated above. This leads to increased plaque deposits in the intimal wall of major peripheral arteries, mainly in the lower body. This may cause a stenosis or occlusion, leading to claudication during exercise, or in serious cases a bout of ischemia causing tissue death which may ultimately result in gangrene or amputation becoming necessary

c) One state based intervention strategies is the active kids voucher. The first 2000 days of life are defined as a high risk period for developing overweight and obesity, which this intervention aims to address. By providing money for children to participate in sports, they will increase their energy expenditure whilst also developing physical literacy and exercise self-efficacy, which may encourage them to participate in more physical activity outside of the program and into adulthood. By increasing physical activity and energy expenditure they are less likely to be in a chronic positive energy balance and become overweight or obese.¬†

Another intervention strategy is the use of a health star rating system on packaging and nutritional information on the back. By having an easy to understand star system and then more detailed information for those who understand, consumers are able to make more health conscious choices to prevent the development of a chronic positive energy balance which leads to overweight and obesity.¬†

A combination of aerobic exercise, resistance training, and both preventative and relieving medications can be used to effectively manage asthma.
When it comes to aerobic exercise, 3-7 sessions a week of 30-60 minutes can help strengthen the lungs and heart to increase blood and oxygen flow to and from the lungs and muscles. It is best to avoid aerobic exercise in a cool, dry environment - as this leads to inflammation and restriction of the airways - so swimming is a great form of exercise, as the pool provides humid, warm air. Avoiding doing cardio outdoors, particularly in cold mornings or evenings is a good idea to avoid the airway irritation.¬†
Resistance training can also be helpful, as it leads to increased cardiac output, leading to better oxygen and blood-flow througout the body.
Preventative medications are typically corticosteroids, and they are taken regularly to mitigate inflammation of the airways and mucus production - they do not provide immediate relief rather, they work over time to manage symptoms
Reliever medications are short-term medications that provide immediate relief, the best example being a ventolin inhaler. These work through bronchodilation, opening up the airways to ease restriction.

Myocardial Infarction - this can lead to sudden death if severe enough, or in less severe cases, necrosis of the heart tissues, leading to long-term CVD
Stroke - This can cause brain damage leading to partial paralysis and other neurological issues
Hypertension - this can lead to poor blood circulation, meaning muscle and organ tissues will get less oxygen, which can lead to tissue necrosis. Furthermore, hypertension can lead to left ventricular hypertrophy
